State government

State Data Overview

California's state government collects revenue into the General Fund (flexible, mostly income and sales tax) and special funds (earmarked, e.g. gas taxes for roads). Spending also includes bond funds and federal funds.

Sources (all fetched by scripts/fetch_*.py, listed with hashes in data/raw/MANIFEST.csv):

  • Legislative Analyst's Office (LAO) historical revenues, 1950-51 to present, and historical expenditures, 1984-85 to present. These come from Department of Finance and State Controller data.
  • State Controller's Office (SCO) Cities, Counties and Special Districts annual reports (revenues and expenditures, FY2002-03 on), via the SCO's open-data API.
  • BLS CPI-U (via FRED) for inflation, and FRED/Census California population. Census files for county FIPS codes and boundaries.

Caveats

  • The revenue series has a break between 2015-16 and 2016-17: LAO publishes the two periods under different accounting categories, so levels shift slightly. Charts mark the break.
  • 2018-19 personal income and sales tax figures in LAO's file are misaligned; those cells are replaced with DOF Schedule 3 totals (all funds). Every comparison and repair is logged in data/processed/revenue_reconciliation.csv.
  • Local data (SCO) ends at FY2023-24 and excludes K-12 school districts and community colleges, which report to the Department of Education. K-12 districts are covered separately from Census data (FY1992-2024); community colleges are not covered.
  • The newest years (shaded "estimate") are budget estimates and proposals, not closed books.
  • Real dollars use CPI-U (US city average) and the latest complete fiscal year as the base.

State Spending in More Detail

The state-spending page groups the budget into broad areas. This page opens those areas up: first by type of spending, then by department within each major area.

How to read it

  • Type of spending: *State operations* is what state departments spend to run themselves (mostly pay and operating costs); *local assistance* is money the state sends on to local governments, schools and individuals (for example Medi-Cal payments to health providers and aid to school districts); *capital outlay* is buildings and construction.
  • Departments change names. The Legislative Analyst's Office renames and reorganizes departments, many of them in FY2013-14. Successors of the same function are chained (for example Department of Health Services and then the Department of Health Care Services) in ca_taxes.state.DEPARTMENT_CHAINS. Splits and mergers, such as Mental Health moving into State Hospitals, are not chained, so some lines still begin or end in a year when a department was reorganized.
  • All funds (general, special, federal and bond). Federal money passes through the state in several areas; see the federal page.
  • Years after FY2025 are budget estimates (shaded).

Inside each area

Top departments in each major area (up to 8, the rest grouped). Use the buttons for nominal, inflation-adjusted, per-person and share views.

Local government

Local Government Revenue

Cities, counties and special districts report finances to the State Controller's Office (SCO). Fiscal years 2002-03 on.

Read this first

  • Not included: K-12 school districts and community colleges report to the Department of Education, not the SCO, so they are not here. Most property tax ultimately funds schools, so these charts understate total local tax collection. County and city tax charts below show what cities and counties themselves receive. K-12 districts have their own page (Census data) in the next section; community colleges are not covered anywhere on this site yet.
  • Double counting: counties receive large state and federal aid ("intergovernmental"), which also shows up in state spending. Do not add state and local totals without netting this out.
  • Reporting break: SCO changed its category format in FY2016-17, so some groups shift at the dotted line. Internal service funds and fund-type categories (special districts) only exist after the change.
  • Values are as reported by each government (SCO does not audit them), in nominal dollars unless the toggle says otherwise.

Local Taxes

Taxes collected by cities and counties, by type. SCO classifies franchise fees under taxes; they're shown separately here. 'Property tax in lieu of VLF' replaced the vehicle license fee revenue the state cut in 2004.

State and local taxes together

State taxes (all funds) next to city and county taxes. Excludes school districts (see the school page) and special districts, so local taxes are understated.

Property tax by recipient

Property tax collected by each kind of local government, 2003 on. The school-district series is from the Census (see the school page); city and county are SCO. Special districts (fire, water, parks) and community colleges also get property tax but are not separable in the data used here, so the total is understated. 'Property tax in lieu of VLF' is excluded.

Local Government Spending

By function. Cities and counties report spending in functional groups that SCO redefined in FY2016-17; this page maps both eras onto one set of groups using the finest reported label (see src/ca_taxes/local.py). City utilities, sanitation and transportation moved between categories at the break, so treat jumps at the dotted line as reporting, not policy.

Special districts

Water, power, hospital, fire, transit and other special districts, by activity (top 12 by cumulative spending).

City spending in more detail (FY2018 on)

The SCO reports city spending by individual function (police, fire, parks, streets...) only since its reporting change, so this finer view covers FY2018 to FY2024. Governmental functions only; city utilities, debt and internal service funds are left out. Top 14 functions by total spending.

K-12 School Districts

California's roughly 1,000 school districts spend about half as much as all cities and counties combined. They report to the Department of Education and the Census Bureau rather than the State Controller, so they come from a separate source: the Census Annual Survey of School System Finances, fiscal years 1992-2024 (FY2024 = school year 2023-24).

Read this first

  • State aid dominates and is not new money: roughly half of district revenue is state aid (mostly Proposition 98), which is already counted in state spending. Do not add it to state totals; the burden page uses only the districts' own local taxes.
  • Local property tax: the "Local property tax" layer is what districts collect directly. Part of it exists because the state shifted property tax from cities, counties and special districts to schools in 1992-93 (ERAF) and later years, so the local mix reflects state decisions.
  • Break at FY2019: Census reclassified over 900 California charter schools (those whose charters are held by non-governmental entities) out of the school systems it surveys, so district revenue, spending and enrollment all step down that year. Marked with a dotted line. Per-pupil lines also jump there: enrollment falls by more than spending, and Census notes the state raised its contributions to school employee pensions that year.
  • FY1994 is missing: the Census file for that year covers only 258 of about 1,080 districts, so it is left out and lines cross the gap.
  • Not included: community colleges (also Proposition 98) are not in this survey. County offices of education are included as districts.
  • Totals follow Census' published state tables: transfers between school systems are excluded from both revenue and spending. Fiscal year ends June 30; the survey's FY2024 is the school year ending in 2024.

Per pupil

Spending and revenue per enrolled student, in constant dollars (fall enrollment as reported in the survey). Enrollment peaked around 2005 and was roughly flat to 2018; the drop in FY2019 is mostly the charter-school reclassification, not lost students.

K-12 Spending: Salaries, Pensions, Benefits and Supplies

Where does a school dollar go? The Department of Education collects every district's, county office's and charter school's year-end accounts under one code structure (SACS), with each dollar coded by what was bought (the object: teacher pay, pensions, supplies...) and what it was for (the function: classroom, administration, buses...). This page uses the statewide totals for school years 2003-04 to the latest (scripts/fetch_cde_sacs.py). Fiscal year is the year the school year ends.

Read this first

  • Scope: district, county-office and charter spending that files in SACS (almost all of it), all funds except pass-through, internal-service and fiduciary funds. Transfers between agencies and funds, and indirect-cost transfers, are removed so money is not counted twice. These are unaudited actuals. Community colleges are not included. Charter schools that file only the short alternative form are not in the totals.
  • Pensions here are what school *employers* pay into the teachers' (STRS) and classified employees' (PERS) retirement systems. California's budget also pays into the teachers' retirement fund on the state's own account; that is not in school ledgers and is shown separately below.
  • Matches Census, roughly: after removing debt principal (which Census leaves out), the totals here are within 1 to 5% of the Census school-spending figures on the school page (the gap widens after FY2019, when Census dropped about 900 charter schools that SACS still includes), but they are different surveys, so use this page for the *breakdown* and that one for the level.
  • Groupings (for example which object codes count as pensions) are in src/ca_taxes/school.py.

For every dollar of salary

Benefits paid per dollar of pay (certificated plus classified salaries), by type. Pension contributions rose sharply with the state's 2014 plan to close the teachers' retirement funding gap, which raised the rate employers pay.

What the data show: employer pension contributions (STRS and PERS) were about 8.5 cents per dollar of salary from 2004 to 2014 and about 25 cents by 2024, rising each year from 2015 to 2019, after the state's 2014 plan to close the teachers' retirement funding gap raised employer rates. As a share of all K-12 spending, pensions rose from 4.4% to 11.0%. Teachers' salaries fell from 31% to 23% of spending (and from 64% to 50% of classroom-instruction spending) while health insurance stayed roughly flat at 12 to 15 cents per dollar of pay. Spending on books and supplies stayed near 4% of the total (5% of classroom instruction). These shares are of total spending including capital projects and debt service; the 2020-2024 totals also include one-time federal pandemic relief.

Staff pay, benefits and everything else, in detail

The next three charts split the groups into their parts: who is paid, which benefits, and what the non-staff dollars buy.

What the money is for

The same spending by function. Instruction is the classroom (including special education); the other functions are the supports around it.

Inside the classroom

What classroom instruction itself is made of: of every dollar coded to instruction (including special education), how much is teacher pay, other staff pay, pensions, other benefits, and supplies?

A school dollar, then and now

Share of total K-12 spending in each category, in the first and latest years and one in between.

The state's own pension contribution

The state budget pays into the teachers' retirement fund separately from what school employers contribute. The two together are the public cost of school-employee pensions through these systems (STRS and PERS employer contributions plus the state's STRS payment). The state's payment covers STRS members in community colleges as well as K-12, so it slightly overstates the K-12 share.

County Maps: Local Taxes and Spending per Person

For each county: taxes collected by the county government plus every city in it, divided by the county's population. San Francisco (a combined city-county) is reported as a city by the SCO and added from there. Excludes school and special districts. Latest year available, nominal dollars.

Putting it together

Total Taxes per Person

State taxes plus city, county and K-12 school district taxes, per Californian. This counts taxes California governments *collect*, not what households pay (federal taxes are excluded, and some state tax is paid by businesses and visitors).

Left out: special districts and community colleges. School districts here means local property and other local taxes only; the state aid they receive (about half of school revenue) is already counted in state spending.

As a share of personal income

Taxes collected divided by total personal income of California residents (BEA, via FRED; fiscal-year average of quarterly rates). This is a rough yardstick of how big government's take is relative to the economy, not an average household tax rate: businesses, visitors and non-residents also pay California taxes, and income here excludes corporate profits retained by firms.

Property tax and Proposition 13

Property Tax and Assessed Values

Property tax is California's largest local tax, and since Proposition 13 (1978) it is set by assessed value rather than market value. The rate is capped at 1% of assessed value plus voter-approved local debt, and a property's assessed value can rise at most 2% a year while its owner holds it; it resets to market value when ownership changes or new construction is added. This page uses the Board of Equalization's (BOE) annual roll statistics, which are public through its open-data API (scripts/fetch_boe.py).

Read this first

  • Short history: the BOE publishes county tables from the 2000 roll, statewide summaries (with levies and tax rates) from 2009, tax allocations from 2012, and single-family detail from 2015. Anything earlier needs old annual-report PDFs not used here.
  • Timing: a roll is the value on January 1 of a year and funds the fiscal year that ends the following June. Charts labelled "fiscal year" use that following year; charts compared with home prices use the January 1 year.
  • Home prices are the FHFA all-transactions house price index for California (FRED), first-quarter values, a measure of residential prices only. Assessed value also includes commercial, industrial and agricultural property, new construction and personal property, so the two are not like for like.
  • Net assessed value here is after exemptions other than the homeowners' exemption (about 1% of the total), as BOE publishes it in Table 5.

Assessed value versus home prices

Both lines are indexed to 2000 = 100. The CPI line is the fiscal-year average CPI-U for the year the roll funds.

What the data show (2000 to 2025 rolls): statewide assessed value rose about 3.9 times and California house prices about 3.7 times, so over the whole period they moved together. The difference is timing. Assessed value rose more slowly than prices in the run-up years (every year from 2001 to 2006, plus 2014 and 2021-2022), and held up when prices fell: prices dropped about 40% from their 2007 peak to 2012, while assessed value slipped about 4% from its 2008 peak to its 2010 low. Since 2012, prices have risen about 2.5 times and assessed value about 2.1 times. Assessed value responds to turnover and new construction as well as to the 2% cap, so this chart shows the net effect, not the effect of Proposition 13 alone.

Levies and the average tax rate

The amount levied on property and the average rate across all property, statewide (2009 on).

Who receives the property tax

BOE allocations of levies to cities, counties, schools and other districts (2012 on). These do not match the Census school-district figures on the school page (FY2024 school-purposes levies here are about 1.7 times the K-12 property tax revenue Census reports). BOE's school group is broader than K-12 districts and levies are not cash collected; the difference is not reconciled here.

The single-family home

Average assessed value per single-family parcel (2015 on). Counties are the six with the most single-family parcels. A parcel's assessed value is what it is taxed on, not what it would sell for.

By county

Compound yearly growth of net assessed value from the 2000 roll to the latest roll, and the average assessed value of a single-family parcel on the latest roll. Colors are capped at the 5th and 95th percentiles; hover shows exact values.

Federal dollars

Federal Dollars: Out and Back In

How much federal tax is collected in California, and how much federal money comes back as benefits, pay and funds to California governments? This page shows several pieces of that picture. It is not a complete balance of payments and should not be read as one.

What is here

  • Taxes out: federal tax collections attributed to California by the IRS (Data Book Table 5, federal fiscal years ending September 30). The IRS assigns each payment to the state where it was filed or deposited, so a multi-state employer's withholding or corporate tax can land in its home state. Includes individual income and payroll taxes, corporate income tax, excise, estate and gift taxes.
  • Money back in, to people: government benefits paid to Californians and federal civilian and military pay (Bureau of Economic Analysis, calendar years). Programs that are federal by design are marked federal; Medicaid and unemployment insurance are shared with the state, and BEA's "other" benefits mix levels of government.
  • Money back in, to governments: federal funds spent by the state, and federal aid received by counties, cities and school districts (from the state, SCO and Census data on the earlier pages).

What is not here: federal contracts and procurement (defense, NASA, research), most grants to universities and businesses, interest on federal debt, tax breaks and deductions, and anything paid to Californians that BEA does not classify as a government transfer. Those omissions mean the "back in" side is understated. Social Security and Medicare are funded by dedicated taxes and are not designed to balance state by state; California's age mix, income and industries all affect where taxes and benefits land.

Timing: IRS years are federal fiscal years (October to September); BEA years are calendar years. They are lined up by the year number, which overlaps about nine months. All dollar values below use the same CPI and population series as the rest of the site.

California share of US federal collections (%), selected years: {1998: 11.3, 2008: 11.6, 2018: 13.2, 2022: 14.2, 2023: 12.1, 2024: 15.8, 2025: 14.4}

California's share of national collections dips in FY2023 and jumps in FY2024. This is consistent with the IRS postponing 2022 filing and payment deadlines for California (winter storms) into the fall of 2023, which moved payments from FY2023 into FY2024; the series is shown as published, so read those two years together.

Federal benefits and pay received by Californians

BEA personal current transfer receipts from governments, plus pay for federal civilian employees and the military, calendar years. Medicaid, unemployment insurance and the 'other' group include state and local money.

Taxes out versus benefits and pay back in, per person

Three measures in constant dollars per Californian. 'Federal programs and pay' counts only programs that are federal by design. The dashed line adds Medicaid and unemployment insurance, which are shared with the state, so it overstates the federal share of those programs. None of the lines includes procurement or grants to organizations.

Federal funds received by California governments

Federal money received by the state, counties, cities and school districts. These lines overlap and must not be added: state spending of federal funds includes money passed to counties and schools, and much county federal aid is public assistance and health programs that also run through the state budget. Counties and cities start in 2003 (SCO).

The state's federal funds jump in FY2020-21 almost entirely because of two areas: the Employment Development Department, which pays unemployment benefits ($141B of federal funds that year versus $7B in 2019), and K-12 education ($27B versus $8B). Neither is a lasting change in the level of federal support; see the by-area chart below.

Federal funds in the state budget

Federal money the state spends, by area (all years from the state's historical expenditure data). The estimate shading marks budget proposals.

Explore

City and County Explorer

Pick any of California's 482 cities or 57 counties and see taxes and spending per resident over time, then compare cities side by side. Fiscal years 2003-2024, from the State Controller's Office (SCO), in constant dollars.

How to read it

  • Taxes are what the city or county itself levies (property, sales, hotel, utility users, business license, franchise and other taxes). Spending is everything it spends, including enterprise services such as water, power, airports and hospitals, which many cities run and others leave to special districts. High spending per person often reflects those services, not higher taxes or waste.
  • Per person uses the population the government reports to the SCO. San Francisco is both a city and a county and appears here as a city. Population is the SCO's own estimate, not the Census count; two cities' populations are swapped in some SCO years (Mt. Shasta and Mountain View) and are corrected here (population_repaired in data/processed/local_entities.csv).
  • Incomplete picture: residents also pay county, school, special-district and state taxes not shown for a city. Counties spend on behalf of everyone in them, including cities' residents.
  • The SCO changed its reporting format in FY2016-17, so spending (but much less so taxes) can shift at that year.

Highest and lowest taxes per person

Cities with at least 25,000 residents, latest year (nominal dollars). The top is tourist and commercial centers (Beverly Hills, Palm Springs, Santa Monica, Monterey) and Bay Area cities, plus San Francisco, which is a combined city-county; part of the gap is visitors, workers and shoppers who pay tax but are not counted as residents. The bottom is mostly inland suburbs and lower-income cities in the Inland Empire and Central Valley.
